standard.title: Angle relationships
standard.description: Identify the relationships between angles on a straight line, angles at a point and vertically opposite angles; use these to determine unknown angles, communicating reasoning
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can estimate, construct and measure angles in degrees using a protractor (AC9M5M04). They understand acute, obtuse, straight, and reflex angles and can measure them. They have not yet identified geometric relationships between angles at a point or on a line, or used these to determine unknown angles.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify the relationships between angles on a straight line, at a point, and vertically opposite; use these to determine unknown angles; communicate their reasoning.

nodes.label: Angles on a straight line
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that angles on a straight line sum to 180° and use this to find an unknown angle.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify angles on a straight line; state that they sum to 180°; calculate at least four unknown angles using the straight-line relationship; verify using measurement.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the straight-line relationship to diagrams with two or three angles on a line; explain why the angles sum to 180° (a straight line is a half-rotation); apply to problem contexts involving straight line segments in diagrams.
wider: Investigate supplementary angles in different geometric figures — in a triangle, in a parallelogram — and identify where the straight-line relationship appears
Explore why the straight-line angle sum is 180° using rotation reasoning: a full rotation is 360°, a straight line is half

response_modes.reason: Students often apply the 180° rule without understanding why it holds. The rotation-based justification (straight angle = half turn = 180°) needs explicit scaffolding before students can communicate reasoning rather than just state the rule.

nodes.hinge_reason: The straight-line relationship is used as a step within the vertically-opposite proof (Node 3) and within all Node 4 multi-step problems. Students who apply 180° as a rote rule without understanding the rotation basis will be unable to identify when and why to apply it in complex diagrams.
success_criteria: Student states the angle relationship for angles on a straight line.
Student correctly finds an unknown angle on a straight line and explains the reasoning.

nodes.label: Angles at a point
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that angles at a point sum to 360° and use this to find unknown angles.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify angles at a point in a diagram; state that they sum to 360°; calculate at least three unknown angles using the relationship.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the angles-at-a-point relationship to diagrams with two, three, and four angles at a point; connect to the full-rotation concept; apply to context problems involving directions, clock faces, and geometric diagrams.
wider: Investigate why clock angles at 3-hour intervals are all 90° using angles-at-a-point reasoning
Explore compass bearing contexts: if you turn 135° clockwise from North, what direction are you facing? Use angles-at-a-point reasoning.
success_criteria: Student states the angle relationship for angles at a point.
Student correctly finds an unknown angle at a point and shows the calculation.

nodes.label: Vertically opposite angles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify vertically opposite angles in a diagram and use the property that they are equal to find unknown angles.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the two pairs of vertically opposite angles when two lines intersect; state that vertically opposite angles are equal; find unknown vertically opposite angles in at least three diagrams.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the vertically opposite angle property in combination with straight-line and at-a-point relationships; explain why vertically opposite angles are equal using straight-line reasoning; apply to multi-angle diagrams.
wider: Investigate whether vertically opposite angles remain equal when lines are not straight — explore with curved intersecting lines and discuss
Explore where vertically opposite angles appear in design, architecture, and tiling — identify at least two real-world examples

response_modes.reason: Students often accept that vertically opposite angles are equal as a stated fact without understanding the proof. Developing the reasoning (both angles are supplementary to the same angle, so they must be equal) establishes a proof habit that is foundational for secondary geometry.

nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the proof that vertically opposite angles are equal (via straight-line relationships) is required for Node 4, where students must identify and apply all three relationships in combination. Students who know the rule without the reasoning cannot construct the multi-step justification required at Node 4.
success_criteria: Student identifies vertically opposite angle pairs in a diagram.
Student uses the property to find unknown angles and explains why the angles are equal.

nodes.label: Combining angle relationships to solve problems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify which angle relationships apply in a multi-step diagram and use a combination of relationships to find multiple unknown angles, communicating their reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Find all unknown angles in a diagram requiring at least two different angle relationships; state which relationship is used at each step.
nodes.typical_width: Solve multi-step angle problems systematically, recording the relationship used at each stage; communicate reasoning clearly including which relationship justifies each step; verify by checking that all angles in the diagram are consistent.
wider: Design a complex angle diagram with several unknowns and write step-by-step solutions for a partner to verify
Investigate angles in First Nations Australian art and design — identify angle relationships appearing in traditional patterns and describe them using geometric vocabulary

response_modes.reason: Multi-step angle problems require students to coordinate all three relationships, identify which applies at each step, and communicate the reasoning chain. The integration of reasoning across steps — not just applying individual rules — is the endpoint skill.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Angle reasoning in complex diagrams is foundational for secondary geometry. The skill of identifying which relationship applies and constructing a reasoning chain rewards deliberate practice and transfers broadly.
success_criteria: Student correctly finds all unknown angles in a diagram using at least two different angle relationships.
Student communicates the reasoning, naming the relationship used at each step.
